title: Vinod Khosla Buys Seattle Seahawks for Record $9.6 Billion, Biggest NFL Sale in History
excerpt: The Indian-American venture capitalist and Sun Microsystems co-founder outbid rival groups to acquire the defending Super Bowl champions from the Paul G. Allen Estate.
body:
• Indian-origin venture capitalist Vinod Khosla has agreed to buy the Seattle Seahawks for a record $9.612 billion, the highest price ever paid for an NFL franchise
  • The deal is the second-most expensive sports team sale in history, behind only the Los Angeles Lakers' $10 billion sale in 2025
  • Khosla's wife will serve as the controlling owner, and the family must divest a 3.1% stake in the San Francisco 49ers before the sale is finalized
  • The purchase marks a milestone for Indian-origin entrepreneurs in global sports ownership, with another Indian-origin billionaire, Aditya Mittal, among the competing bidders

A Record-Breaking Deal

Vinod Khosla, the Indian-American billionaire and co-founder of Sun Microsystems, has agreed to purchase the Seattle Seahawks from the Paul G. Allen Estate for $9.612 billion, shattering the previous NFL franchise sale record of $6.05 billion set by the Washington Commanders in 2023.

The deal, brokered by Allen & Co., positions Khosla's family at the helm of the defending Super Bowl champions. The Seahawks defeated the New England Patriots in Super Bowl LX in February, making the franchise one of the NFL's most coveted properties. Khosla's wife will serve as the controlling owner, according to Front Office Sports, which first reported the specifics of the ownership structure.

From IIT Delhi to NFL Ownership

Khosla, 71, was born in New Delhi and studied electrical engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi before earning an MBA from Stanford University. He co-founded Sun Microsystems in 1982 and went on to establish Khosla Ventures, one of Silicon Valley's most influential venture capital firms. Forbes estimates his net worth at approximately $13.8 billion.

The sale process attracted multiple bidders, including a group led by Aditya Mittal, the CEO of steel and mining giant ArcelorMittal and himself of Indian origin. The presence of two Indian-origin billionaires among the final bidders for an NFL franchise underscores the growing economic power of the Indian diaspora in American business and sports.

The Allen Estate's Legacy

Paul Allen purchased the Seahawks in 1997 specifically to prevent the franchise from relocating out of Seattle. He owned the team until his death at age 65 in 2018, after which his sister Jody Allen managed the franchise through his estate. Allen's trust directed the eventual sale of both the Seahawks and the NBA's Portland Trail Blazers, with proceeds earmarked for philanthropic efforts.

The Seahawks sale process drew what Allen & Co. described as "very robust interest," though insiders noted the final set of qualified bidders was selective rather than expansive. NFL ownership rules require a single individual to hold at least 30% of a team's value, limit ownership groups to 25 investors, and cap debt financing — constraints that narrow the field even among the ultra-wealthy.

Divesting From the 49ers

One complication Khosla must resolve: he currently holds a 3.1% limited partner interest in the San Francisco 49ers, valued at roughly $267 million based on the franchise's estimated $8.6 billion valuation. NFL rules prohibit ownership stakes in more than one franchise, so Khosla must divest that interest before the Seahawks sale is finalized and approved by league owners.

What It Means for the Diaspora

The acquisition adds Khosla to a growing roster of Indian-origin figures in major American sports ownership. The deal's sheer scale — second only to the Lakers' $10 billion sale among all global sports transactions — signals that Indian-origin entrepreneurs have moved well beyond the technology sector into the highest echelons of American cultural and sporting institutions.

For the Seahawks, the transition marks a new chapter after nearly three decades under Allen family stewardship. The Khosla family has signaled an intention to maintain continuity, keeping current general manager John Schneider and head coach Mike Macdonald involved in the ownership transition process. Both executives participated in interviews with prospective ownership groups during the team's minicamp earlier this summer.
